title: Diagnostic: where should you actually start?
intro: Fourteen questions across the seven modules. This is not a beginner test: it exists to decide which modules you can skip and which need real work. Answer honestly and do not look things up — a wrong answer here only saves you time later.
scoring: A module at 75% or above is marked strong and deprioritised. Below that, it goes on your path. Your interview date and accelerated mode decide the order.

questions.prompt: A host has 10.20.30.200/26. Which statement is true?
options: The gateway must be within 10.20.30.192-10.20.30.254
The host cannot communicate because /26 is invalid for that range
The broadcast address is 10.20.30.255
The gateway must be 10.20.30.1 because that is the first address in the subnet
questions.explanation: A /26 gives blocks of 64: 10.20.30.192/26 covers .192-.255, so the usable range is .193-.254 and the gateway must be inside it. 10.20.30.255 is the broadcast.

why_wrong.3: The gateway must be in the same subnet as the host, which for this host starts at .192.
why_wrong.1: A /26 is perfectly valid inside a /24.
why_wrong.2: For 10.20.30.200/26 the block is .192-.255, so .255 is the broadcast, but the statement about the gateway is the only fully correct one.

questions.prompt: Two hosts on the same switch are in 10.0.10.0/24 and 10.0.20.0/24 with no router. What happens when the first pings the second?
options: The switch sends an ICMP redirect
ARP resolves the target and the ping succeeds
The ping fails: different subnets need a router even on the same switch
The ping succeeds because the switch forwards at Layer 2
questions.explanation: The host decides the destination is off-link and ARPs for its gateway. With no gateway there is nothing to ARP for, so the ping fails before any frame reaches the other host.

why_wrong.3: The sender never sends to the other host's MAC, so switching is irrelevant.
why_wrong.0: The host has no route, so no packet is generated for a redirect to apply to.
why_wrong.1: ARP for the target is never attempted because the mask says it is off-link.

questions.prompt: A trunk carries VLANs 10 and 20 and the native VLAN is 1. An untagged frame arrives on the trunk. Which VLAN does it belong to?
options: It is dropped
VLAN 1
VLAN 20
VLAN 10
questions.explanation: Untagged frames on a trunk belong to the native VLAN. That is exactly why a native VLAN mismatch silently merges two VLANs.

why_wrong.3: Tagged frames carry their own VLAN id; only untagged traffic uses the native VLAN.
why_wrong.0: It is not dropped, it is assigned to the native VLAN — the security problem with mismatched natives.

questions.prompt: A switch floods a frame to every port in the VLAN. Which case is this?
options: The source MAC is unknown
The destination MAC is in the MAC table on another port
The destination MAC is on the ingress port
The destination MAC is unknown or a broadcast
questions.explanation: Flooding happens for broadcast, multicast and unknown unicast. Known unicast is forwarded to one port, and a destination on the ingress port is filtered.

why_wrong.1: That is a normal forward, not a flood.
why_wrong.0: An unknown source is learned, not a reason to flood.

questions.prompt: A client on VLAN 30 gets no DHCP address; the server is in another subnet. What is the most likely missing element?
options: A longer lease time
A static route on the client
A DHCP relay (ip helper-address) on the VLAN 30 gateway
A second DHCP scope on the server
questions.explanation: DHCP starts with a broadcast, which cannot cross a router. A relay converts it to unicast with giaddr so the server knows which scope to use.

why_wrong.0: Lease duration affects renewals, not whether the first DISCOVER reaches a server.
why_wrong.3: The server needs a scope, but without a relay it never sees the request.
why_wrong.1: The client has no address yet, so it cannot have a static route.

questions.prompt: dig returns status NXDOMAIN with an SOA in the authority section. What does that tell you?
options: The name exists but has no record of that type
The queried name does not exist in the zone that answered
DNSSEC validation failed
The DNS server is unreachable
questions.explanation: NXDOMAIN is authoritative absence, and the SOA identifies the zone plus the negative-caching TTL. NODATA (name exists, type does not) is a different case with NOERROR.

why_wrong.3: An unreachable server produces a timeout, not a response with an SOA.
why_wrong.0: That is NODATA: NOERROR with an empty answer section.

questions.prompt: Small HTTP requests succeed instantly; a large upload hangs until timeout. Ping is clean. What do you test first?
options: Whether the server's disk is full
Whether DNS resolution is slow
The TLS certificate expiry
A DF ping sweep to find the path MTU
questions.explanation: Failures that scale with payload size are the MTU signature. ping -M do -s with increasing sizes finds the largest passing size.

why_wrong.0: Disk pressure would not correlate with request size while small requests succeed.
why_wrong.1: A slow lookup affects the first request regardless of size.
why_wrong.2: A certificate problem affects every request, not just large ones.

questions.prompt: A connection attempt returns an immediate 'connection refused'. What does that mean?
options: The host actively rejected it — often nothing listening, or a firewall REJECT
A firewall is silently dropping the packets
The name could not be resolved
The route to the host is missing
questions.explanation: A refusal is an active response: RST (nothing listening) or an ICMP administratively-prohibited (REJECT). DROP gives a timeout instead.

why_wrong.1: A silent DROP produces a timeout, which feels completely different.
why_wrong.3: A missing route gives 'network unreachable', not a refusal.
why_wrong.2: A resolution failure never reaches the TCP connection stage.

questions.prompt: A router has 10.0.0.0/8 via A (metric 10) and 10.1.0.0/16 via B (metric 200). Where does traffic to 10.1.5.5 go?
options: Load-shared across both
Via A
Via B
Dropped
questions.explanation: Longest prefix match compares prefix length before metric, so /16 beats /8 regardless of the worse metric.

why_wrong.0: A single route is chosen per packet (ECMP requires equal prefixes and metrics).

questions.prompt: A branch can ping HQ but HQ cannot ping the branch. The branch router's table is correct. What is the most likely cause?
options: The branch link is down
The branch hosts have the wrong gateway
A duplex mismatch on the branch uplink
A missing return route for the branch subnet on the HQ side
questions.explanation: One-way failure with a correct forward path is asymmetric routing: the far side has no route back to the source subnet.

why_wrong.0: Then the branch could not ping HQ either.
why_wrong.1: Then the branch host could not send at all.
why_wrong.2: A duplex mismatch degrades throughput but does not produce a clean one-way failure.

questions.prompt: A file is -rw-r----- root:app and the process runs as user app whose primary group is app. Can it read the file?
options: Yes, but only if it is also in the root group
Yes — it is not the owner, so group bits apply and group has r
No — only the owner can read a 640 file
No — group app has no execute bit
questions.explanation: Mode evaluation stops at the first matching class: owner, then group, then others. The process is in group app, which has r.

why_wrong.2: Group read is exactly what 640 grants.
why_wrong.3: Execute is needed on directories, not to read a regular file.
why_wrong.0: Group membership is what matters, and app is the group.

questions.prompt: EACCES persists after fixing the mode bits. ls -Z shows user_home_t for a file under /etc. What is the correct action?
options: Relabel the path with restorecon (or an fcontext rule plus restorecon)
Run the service as root
Set SELinux to permissive
chmod 777 the file
questions.explanation: SELinux is a second control. restorecon applies the policy's expected type to the path so the service domain is allowed to read it.

why_wrong.3: Mode bits are not the blocker and this weakens the system.
why_wrong.2: Disables the control instead of fixing the label.
why_wrong.1: Does not change the file's label and violates least privilege.

questions.prompt: Load average is 40, CPU utilisation is 6%, and iowait is 88%. What is the most likely explanation?
options: There is a memory leak
The CPU is oversubscribed and needs more cores
The load average is wrong
Many tasks are blocked in uninterruptible IO waits, not competing for CPU
questions.explanation: Load counts runnable plus uninterruptible tasks. High load with low CPU and high iowait means tasks are blocked in the kernel, typically on storage or a network filesystem.

why_wrong.1: CPU is mostly idle; more cores would not help.
why_wrong.0: A leak would show in memory and possibly OOM messages, not iowait.
why_wrong.2: The metric is behaving exactly as documented.

questions.prompt: A process is in state D and does not die after kill -9. Why?
options: The PID was reused
SIGKILL requires root
It is blocked in an uninterruptible kernel wait, so signals are not delivered until the wait ends
systemd restarts it immediately
questions.explanation: Signals are handled on return to user space. A task in D state cannot return until the kernel operation completes, so the signal stays pending.

why_wrong.1: SIGKILL is not privilege-gated beyond normal signal permission.
why_wrong.0: A reused PID would show a different process, usually in S or R.
why_wrong.3: A restart would appear as a new PID, not the same one still in D.

plan_rules.note: Modules at or above the threshold are marked optional revision. Everything below becomes part of the plan, ordered by weight and accelerated mode.
